_what_this_is: The published-controls register: the controls this repo PUBLICLY CLAIMS to enforce.
It is a statement of INTENT, written from the published documents, and it is the
expectation `scripts/mutate.py` checks its mutation catalogue against.
It exists because the expectation used to live inside mutate.py itself, as a dict whose
keys WERE the mutant names, hand-edited beside the mutant table in the same commit. That
check could not fail for the reason it advertised: it derived its expectation from the
artifact it was checking. R17 M22 reproduced the consequence — a tree with four safety
controls physically deleted ran green, killed all 17 mutants, and printed 'every
_how_to_use_it: A control lands with its claim and its mutant in the SAME change: add the entry here,
add the mutant to scripts/mutate.py, and cite the document that makes the claim public.
`published_in` is a provenance pin, not decoration. Each `anchor` is a literal string
that must still appear in the named file, so the register cannot drift away from the
documents it claims to summarise — the same exact-string discipline the mutant table
already uses for source code, applied to claims.
Do NOT delete an entry to make mutate.py green. An entry with no mutant means a control
this repo publicly claims has nothing verifying it, which is the finding, not the noise.
_honest_limit: This makes the completeness check non-circular. It does NOT make it complete, and no
version of it can be: a control that is implemented in code and claimed NOWHERE is
undetectable by any claims-based check. 'Every control we claim has a mutant' is
enforceable. 'Every control the code actually has, has a mutant' is not — that would
mean deriving intent from implementation, which is the circularity being removed.
